newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: U.N. says new Afghan ceasefire plan drawn up.
newsitem.headline: U.N. says new Afghan ceasefire plan drawn up.

text.p: A U.N. peace mission for Afghanistan said on Wednesday it had drawn up a revised plan for a ceasefire to be discussed next week with rival factions locked in battle north of Kabul and elsewhere.

The first draft was discussed at a meeting that special U.N. envoy Norbert Holl held in Islamabad last week with representatives of the radical Islamic Taleban militia and a northern opposition alliance seeking to oust it from Kabul.

Holl left for New York on Wednesday to attend an international conference on Afghanistan set for Monday. No Afghan faction has been invited to the meeting, called by U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali.

Holl's deputy, Francis Okelo, told Reuters that the new draft ceasefire accord had been prepared in consultation with the Taleban and its foes. It proposes formation of a commission representing the rival factions to monitor the ceasefire.
"This will be the stepping-stone, the first step towards demilitarisation (of Kabul) and formation of a broad-based interim government," Okelo said in Peshawar, Pakistan.
Previous efforts to negotiate a ceasefire, which would include arrangements for an exchange of prisoners and bodies, have foundered on differences over what should happen next.
Okelo said the new draft addressed reservations voiced by the feuding factions about the earlier one.
"I am hopeful and optimistic about the success of the talks next week," he said.

Holl said after his November 7 meeting with Taleban acting Foreign Minister Mullah Mohammad Ghous and General Mohammed Paynda, speaking for the northern alliance, that both sides had agreed that a political process should focus on demilitarising Kabul and handing the war-battered city to a neutral force.
But he said they differed on how far the rival forces should pull back from the capital, which the Taleban captured on September 27, and on how a neutral force should be composed.
Ghous said on Friday that the Taleban could withdraw its troops to their bases in Kabul in a mutual pullback of forces from the frontlines, but would not give up the capital.
The Taleban have objected to the possible presence of ousted president Burhanuddin Rabbani at a U.N.-sponsored World Food Summit that opened in Rome on Wednesday.
Taleban-controlled Shariat radio said on Tuesday that Ghous had written to Boutros-Ghali, arguing that Rabbani should be barred from the summit as he no longer represented Afghanistan.
